subcategory: Responsible AI, Human Rights and Safety
oneSentence: The unequal ability of people, organisations or countries to build, access, use or shape AI systems and their benefits.
plainExplanation:
This term describes gaps in who can take part in AI and who benefits from it. Some actors have powerful computers, large amounts of data, skilled staff, funding and influence over standards. Others have little access to these things, or only access as customers of tools built elsewhere.

What goes in are resources and conditions: electricity, internet access, language support, data, compute, money, education, policy capacity and legal protections. Compute means the processing power needed to train or run AI systems. Uneven inputs can make the ability to build, test, govern and benefit from AI uneven too.

What happens next is not just a technical gap. Organisations with more access can create better tools faster, attract more talent, shape markets and set expectations for everyone else. Groups with less access may be left using systems that do not fit their language, context or rights needs, and may have little say in how those systems are designed.

What comes out can be unequal opportunities, dependence on a few providers, weaker local capacity and unfair impacts. The AI divide is related to the digital divide, but it is not the same thing. The digital divide concerns reliable use of digital tools and services more broadly. The AI divide is specifically about access to AI capability, influence, safety capacity and benefits.

everydayAnalogy.title: Tuning a radio across different places
everydayAnalogy.story: Three community centres in different countries try to follow the same radio lesson. One has a strong receiver, stable electricity and a clear signal, so everyone hears the full programme. Another has an older radio and constant interference, so parts of the lesson cut in and out. The third can only catch one distant station in another language, so people hear something, but it does not fully fit their needs.

mapping.aiElement: access to compute, infrastructure and funding
reliable access to useful AI tools and services
barriers such as poor connectivity, limited skills or weak language support

mapping.analogyElement: only one distant station in another language
mapping.aiElement: dependence on AI systems built elsewhere that may not suit local context

everydayAnalogy.limitation: A radio mainly involves receiving a broadcast, while AI also involves creating systems, training staff, setting rules, checking harms and deciding where human judgement must stay in control. The AI divide is therefore not only about getting access to a signal. It is also about power over design, governance, labour conditions and whose needs count.

visual.title: How unequal inputs create an AI divide
visual.learningObjective: Show how differences in infrastructure, skills and influence lead to unequal access to AI benefits and unequal exposure to risks.
visual.description: A left-to-right flow with three columns. Column 1 lists unequal starting conditions. Column 2 shows what those conditions change in practice: building, buying, using and governing AI. Column 3 shows likely outcomes, both benefits for some and disadvantages for others. Read from left to right to see cause and effect.

steps.label: Starting conditions
steps.explanation: People and organisations begin with very different levels of electricity, internet, compute, data, funding, skills, language support and policy capacity.
steps.visualInstruction: Draw seven input boxes in the left column, each with an icon and short label. Use varied fill levels to suggest uneven access.

steps.label: AI capability
steps.explanation: These differences affect who can build models, adapt tools for local needs, evaluate risks and negotiate with providers.
steps.visualInstruction: In the middle column, place four stacked boxes labelled build, adapt, assess, negotiate. Connect every left-column input to these boxes with arrows.

steps.label: Use and governance
steps.explanation: Actors with more capability can deploy AI more widely and shape rules, standards and market expectations. Others may rely on external systems with less local control.
steps.visualInstruction: Add two middle-right boxes labelled deploy and shape rules. Use thicker arrows from the capability boxes to show reinforcing effects.

steps.label: Outcomes
steps.explanation: The result can be better services and economic gains for some, but exclusion, dependence, poor fit, weaker oversight and unfair impacts for others.
steps.visualInstruction: In the right column, split outcomes into two grouped panels: benefits and risks. Use balanced colours, not alarm colours, and connect both from the previous stage.

visual.interaction: Hovering or tapping any left-column input highlights the downstream effects it influences, showing that the divide has multiple causes, not one.
visual.accessibilityDescription: The diagram explains that the AI divide starts with unequal conditions such as electricity, internet, compute, data, funding, skills, language support and policy capacity. These conditions affect who can build AI systems, adapt them to local needs, assess risks and negotiate with providers. That then affects who can deploy AI widely and who can shape rules and standards. The outcomes differ: some gain better services and economic advantage, while others face exclusion, dependence on outside providers, poor local fit, weaker oversight and unfair impacts. The key message is that unequal inputs create unequal capability, which creates unequal influence and unequal results.
visual.reducedMotionDescription: A static three-column flowchart shows starting conditions on the left, AI capability and governance in the middle, and outcomes on the right, with clear arrows connecting causes to effects.

workedExample.scenario: A regional health training network is exploring an AI tool to translate public health guidance into three languages used by clinics in different countries.
workedExample.input: Organisation A has a budget of USD 120,000, two data specialists, approved servers and local language datasets. Organisation B has USD 8,000, one part-time IT officer and no local language data.
process: Organisation A tests three models on approved infrastructure, compares error rates and adds human review by health experts.
Organisation B can only try one low-cost external service and cannot fine-tune it for local terminology.
Organisation A produces draft translations with 92% terminology accuracy in pilot testing; Organisation B gets 68% and many terms remain inconsistent.
Because Organisation A has capacity to evaluate and adapt the system, it can use AI as a supervised aid. Organisation B remains dependent on a tool that fits its needs poorly.
workedExample.result: Both organisations technically 'have AI access', but the quality, safety, local fit and bargaining power are very different. That difference is the AI divide in practice.

unWorkplaceExample.scenario: A UN team wants to summarise submissions to a public consultation that arrived in several languages. A large office has approved tools, multilingual staff and time to test quality. A smaller office has limited budget, little technical support and fewer language resources, so it may depend on a single external tool with less ability to check errors or bias.
unWorkplaceExample.relevance: This matters because uneven AI capacity inside and across organisations can affect whose views are represented accurately, who can evaluate risks and who can benefit from productivity gains.
unWorkplaceExample.caution: Use only approved tools and workflows. Do not paste confidential, personal, protection-sensitive or unpublished submissions into an unapproved public AI service, and keep human review over summaries that inform decisions.

whyItMatters: If people hear about AI only as a new tool, they may miss a deeper question: who gets to build it, shape it, check it and benefit from it. The AI divide affects public services, education, language inclusion, market power, labour conditions and human rights protections. For leaders and programme teams, it changes what is realistic, what is fair and where safeguards are needed. A project can look efficient on paper while quietly increasing dependency on a few providers, excluding low-resource languages or reducing the voice of communities with less technical capacity. Recognising the divide helps organisations plan support, procurement, oversight and capacity-building more responsibly.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: It only means some people do not have internet access.
commonMisconceptions.correction: Internet access is part of the picture, but the AI divide is broader. It also includes access to compute, data, skills, language support, funding, evaluation capacity and influence over design and rules. A group may be online but still have very little power to use AI well or safely.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: If cheap AI tools are available online, the divide disappears.
commonMisconceptions.correction: Low-cost access can help, but it does not remove deeper gaps. Users still need suitable languages, local relevance, staff training, approved infrastructure, legal safeguards and the ability to test quality and harms. Without those, access may be shallow and dependence may increase.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: This is only a problem between rich and poor countries.
commonMisconceptions.correction: The divide can exist within one country, one city or one organisation. Large companies may have far more capacity than small businesses, major languages may be better served than minority languages, and well-funded offices may have stronger oversight than under-resourced ones.

simpleVsTechnical.simple: Some groups can build and use AI much more effectively than others because they have more computing power, money, skills, data and influence.
simpleVsTechnical.technical: The AI divide refers to unequal distribution of the inputs and capabilities needed across the AI lifecycle: access to compute, data, connectivity, energy, specialised talent, evaluation methods, language resources, finance, procurement leverage, governance capacity and participation in standard-setting. These asymmetries affect who can train, fine-tune, deploy, audit and contest AI systems, and who captures economic and social benefits. The term is often discussed alongside the digital divide, but it is narrower in one sense because it focuses on AI-specific capability, and broader in another because it includes power over design, safety testing, oversight and market structure, not only end-user access.

keyTakeaway: The AI divide is not just about who can use AI tools; it is also about who can shape them, check them and benefit from them fairly.

quickCheck.question: Which example best shows an AI divide rather than only a general digital divide?
options: Two schools both have internet, but only one has skilled staff, approved computing resources and local language data to adapt and evaluate an AI tool.
A village has no mobile signal, so residents cannot use online services at all.
An office printer stops working during a meeting.
A team chooses to write a report without any software support.
quickCheck.explanation: The first option shows unequal AI-specific capability: skills, compute, data and evaluation capacity. The second is mainly a broader connectivity problem, which is part of the digital divide. The other two are not examples of this term.

contested: The exact boundary of this term is somewhat unsettled. Some people use it mainly for gaps in compute and technical capacity, while others use it more broadly to include access, governance power, language inclusion and who captures benefits.

issues.problem: The sentence defining the digital divide as being about "access to digital tools and connectivity" is too narrow and contradicts the supplied definition, which also covers reliable use, cost, skills, language, design and safety barriers.
issues.fix: Replace it with: "The digital divide concerns reliable use of digital tools and services more broadly."

issues.problem: The claim "If these inputs are uneven, the ability to build, test, govern and benefit from AI is also uneven" states an automatic causal relationship. Unequal inputs can contribute to unequal capability, but one unequal input does not guarantee that every listed ability is unequal.
issues.fix: Replace it with: "Uneven inputs can make the ability to build, test, govern and benefit from AI uneven too."

issues.problem: The explanation lists eight inputs, but the instruction requests seven boxes. The count is 1 electricity + 1 internet + 1 compute + 1 data + 1 funding + 1 skills + 1 language support + 1 policy capacity = 8 boxes, not 7.
issues.fix: Replace "seven input boxes" with "eight input boxes".

issues.problem: The visual is specified as a three-column flowchart, but this instruction introduces a "middle-right" area. That makes the layout ambiguous and conflicts with the description and reduced-motion alternative.
issues.fix: Replace it with: "In the middle column, add two boxes after capability labelled deploy and shape rules. Use thicker arrows from the capability boxes to show reinforcing effects."

issues.problem: The closing statement says unequal inputs "create" unequal capability, influence and results. This presents a possible pathway as an inevitable mechanism, unlike the more qualified outcome language elsewhere.
issues.fix: Replace the final sentence with: "The key message is that unequal inputs can create unequal capability, influence and results."

issues.problem: Option 0 is the only defensible answer. Option 1 is a general connectivity divide, while options 2 and 3 have no plausible connection to any divide and can be rejected without understanding the term. The distractors therefore make the quiz too easy.
issues.fix: Use these options: ["Two schools both have internet, but only one has skilled staff, approved computing resources and local language data to adapt and evaluate an AI tool.", "Two schools have different internet reliability, affecting all their online services equally.", "A non-AI public service cannot be used effectively with a screen reader.", "An organisation runs a planned programme so staff can maintain existing digital systems with less outside help."]

issues.problem: The explanation correctly identifies option 0, but it does not support meaningful discrimination because the existing final two distractors are irrelevant. With the proposed options, it should explain each distinction.
issues.fix: Replace it with: "The first shows unequal AI-specific capability. The second is a general digital divide. The third concerns accessibility, while the fourth describes capacity-building rather than an AI divide."
